The growth trajectory to reach this length appears to be slow, a characteristic consistent with the species' extended lifespan and the relatively cool waters of its southern hemisphere distribution.

The onset of gonadal activity at this moderate size allows individuals to contribute to the next generation before encountering the elevated mortality risks that larger, more conspicuous fish might face from avian and piscine predators. Puberty occurs after a juvenile period spent primarily in inshore nursery grounds. The extended lifespan, combined with delayed maturity at 25 cm, implies a relatively low annual natural mortality rate, an inference supported by the low gonadic somatic index discussed earlier. The species' iteroparous reproductive strategy — spawning multiple times across a prolonged adult life — spreads the risk of recruitment failure across years. Older, larger females contribute disproportionately to population fecundity, underscoring the importance of protecting the older age classes to maintain the reproductive capacity of the stock under commercial fishing pressure.

The New Zealand turbot's life history is further characterized by a slow pace of life typical of many pleuronectids. The combination of low fecundity per event and iteroparity means that population resilience depends heavily on the survival of adult females across multiple spawning seasons. The species is also subject to variable recruitment, influenced by oceanographic conditions during the pelagic larval phase. Conservation efforts focus on maintaining a balanced age structure to buffer against environmental fluctuations. Future studies should investigate the relationship between body condition and reproductive output to refine stock assessment models.
